metadata.title: Early exit polls: 38 percent approve of Trump, lower than past 4 presidents

sources.text:
🕒 The latest on Trump’s approval rating
Updated November 2, 2026
Donald Trump’s approval rating recently hit an all time low of 36.3 percent. It has since rebounded about a point, and today sits at 38.4 percent. Still, with a disapproval rating of about 59 percent, Trump is ending the midterms in a far worse place than he did during his first term.
The share of Americans who strongly approve of the president is just 21 percent, compared to nearly 49 percent who strongly disapprove. -EMD, 11/2/26
See also: Midterm election forecast, generic congressional ballot dashboard, and Iran War support dashboard.
Paid subscribers get full access to our Election Night livestream with The Argument, GD Politics, and Slow Boring.
This is the landing page for Silver Bulletin presidential approval ratings. We’ll regularly update the charts below as new polls about Donald Trump’s approval rating come in.1 This page is designed to be viewed on the web rather than in our email client or in the Substack app.
Click here for more information on how the average works. The Silver Bulletin average weights more reliable polls heavily — you can find our latest pollster ratings here.
The topline: So, just how popular is Trump?
Our default average reflects a combination of all polls, whether conducted among adults, registered voters or likely voters. If a pollster releases multiple versions of the same survey, we use the all-adult version of the poll before the registered voter version.2 This is because all Americans have a say in how popular the president is — whether or not they vote.
The polls: What do the surveys say?
Each poll gets an “influence” score based on its pollster rating, its sample size, its recency, and how often a pollster is publishing numbers.3 Sometimes, surveys with mediocre pollster ratings have more weight in the model just because they were conducted very recently or polled more people.

sources.news_title: Trump approval stuck near record low as Democrats lead midterm race
See CBS News exit poll results for the 2026 midterm elections
sources.text:
See CBS News exit poll results for the 2026 midterm elections
Note: Results will continue to update throughout the night; please check the CBS News desktop election app for the latest.
South Carolina Senate: Toss-up
CBS News rates the race between GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews a toss-up. Most voters don't think Darline Graham has the right experience to be a U.S. senator. But it's not a dealbreaker for all voters — about a quarter who hold this view are still voting for Graham, who was named to fill the seat held by her late brother, Lindsey Graham.
At the same time, about half of voters say of Andrews that her views are too extreme. And most of those voters are voting against Andrews.
Georgia Senate: Ossoff projected to win
Within 40 minutes of polls closing in Georgia, CBS News projected Ossoff as the winner. Democrat Jon Ossoff is performing very well with Black voters as he defends his seat against GOP Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is on pace to win roughly the same share as when he won his runoff election in 2021.
He is also making some inroads with White voters, early exit polls show.
Most White voters are backing Collins, but this would be a really good performance by a Democrat in Georgia among White voters if this holds.
Also, on balance, more voters view Colllins' views as extreme than Ossoff's views.
Overview of CBS News 2026 exit polls for the midterm elections
President Trump is on track for the lowest approval rating for a president in a midterm election, according to early exit polls. Currently at 38%, it's lower than it was during Mr. Trump's first term, and lower than it was for George W. Bush in 2006 when his party lost both houses of Congress.
Midterm elections have often been a referendum on the sitting president, and this one is no exception. Roughly six in 10 say Mr. Trump is a factor in their vote for the House.
This is being driven largely by voters backing Democrats, who are overwhelmingly motivated by opposition to Mr. Trump.
But for those backing Republicans, it's less about the president. Back in 2018, most Republican voters said their vote was to support Mr. Trump. That figure is lower today.
The president has often told his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot, and for many in the MAGA base, they may be doing just that. Most MAGA Republicans say their vote is to support Mr. Trump, but most non-MAGA Reps say he is not a factor.
The mood of the electorate is a sour one
Voters are just plain not happy.
Current exit polls show roughly three-quarters of voters are at least dissatisfied with the direction of the country. More are angry now about how things are going than they were in 2024, as economic anxiety persists. Those voting for Democrats are particularly likely to be angry.
The issue of the economy and trust in Mr. Trump to fix it helped propel him to victory in 2024, but voters feel no better about the condition of the economy today.
In fact, more voters have negative views of the economy now than they did two years ago, and views of the economy are more in line with what we saw in the 2022 midterms, when the party in power lost seats.
Cost of living: Voters are feeling the pinch
Voters are feeling it in their pocketbooks. They are more than twice as likely to say their finances are worse rather than better, based on early exit polls.
Voters across parties express concern about affording everything from gas to groceries to utilities.
For two consecutive elections, most voters have said inflation caused hardship for their family, including about one in five who describe that hardship as severe.
All this adds up to the cost of living being a major factor for voters across parties, but it's more crucial for those backing Democrats. Immigration enforcement is more crucial for those backing Republicans.
When voters are asked to pick their most important issue from a list, the economy comes out on top, followed by the state of democracy. Those voting for Democrats prioritize the state of democracy — an issue that has long concerned them.
For those backing Republicans, the economy is their most important issue, followed by immigration.
Voters who pick the state of democracy as their top issue are particularly likely to say government corruption is a crucial factor in their vote.
Government corruption: It's a major factor for voters across party lines
Roughly nine in 10 voters nationally say government corruption is a major factor in their vote — about the same as cost of living — and it's crucial to those voting for Democrats.
About six in 10 voters think President Trump puts his own personal interests over the country.
The Iran War
While the war with Iran is less of a factor for voters than the cost of living, the conflict is not popular. Most think the U.S. made the wrong decision to take that military action, including about a quarter of Republicans.
Those most concerned about affording gas are the most likely to disagree with the decision to attack Iran.
Does all this dissatisfaction translate to satisfaction with the party out of power?
Neither political party is viewed favorably by a majority of voters.
About one in five backing Democrats for the House have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party. Most Democrats are motivated by their opposition to Mr. Trump.
And the Democratic Party isn't overwhelmingly seen as the party better able to handle key issues.
Emerging issues
Data centers arose as an issue in this campaign. In all the Senate battlegrounds, majorities oppose the construction of a data center in their community.
More voters see artificial intelligence as doing more to harm society than to help it.
Voter confidence
Large majorities of voters are at least somewhat confident that their votes will be counted accurately both nationwide and in their own states, and that eligible voters will be allowed to vote. But while they are confident in their votes being counted, those voting Republican are far less confident that people who are not eligible to vote will be prevented from voting.
This national exit poll measures the general preference for voters nationwide in their choice for the House of Representatives. The House of Representatives, of course, is elected seat by seat.
A quick note on the states
Mr. Trump's job approval is currently underwater in nearly all the Senate battleground states, according to early exit polls, including in states that he won by double digits in 2024.
In all the Senate battlegrounds, more say their finances are worse, not better, compared to years ago.
And party control of the Senate was on the minds of voters. Majorities of those voting for Republican candidates and those voting for Democrats say which party controls the Senate was a major factor in their vote.
The CBS News exit poll interviewed thousands of voters across the country at polling locations on Election Day and in the weeks leading up to Election Day. This is how the voter polling was conducted.

sources.news_title: Trump scores lowest midterm voter approval numbers ever in CBS exit poll
sources.text:
Trump scores lowest midterm voter approval numbers ever in CBS exit poll
Trump has a worse approval rating than his Democratic rival Joe Biden during the 2022 midterms
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join today
Already a member? Log in
Donald Trump has scored the lowest voter approval rating of any president during the midterm elections in a new exit poll.
Trump’s job approval rating sits at 38 percent, a CBS News exit poll shows. This is down from the 45 percent approval rating in the 2018 midterms during his first term.
It’s also lower than the 44 percent that Joe Biden received in 2022 and the 44 percent that Barack Obama received in 2010. Even George W. Bush, who was in the midst of his “War on Terror” in the 2006 midterms, received a better approval rating than Trump at 43 percent.
Trump has been struggling with his image while trying to use it to boost Republican candidates in the midterms. The president held almost daily rallies last month and told his supporters to pretend he was on the ballot. But even with the support of his base, it may not be enough to keep GOP control of Congress in Tuesday’s elections.
Roughly three-quarters of voters are, at the very least, dissatisfied with the direction the country is going as many struggle with the cost of living — an issue Trump promised to make better during his second term and has come up short on.
Thirty-eight percent of voters feel angry about the state of the country, while another 37 percent feel dissatisfied. Only 18 percent feel satisfied with how things are going, and 7 percent feel enthusiastic.
Trump has long blamed Biden for the state of the economy – even two years after the Democrat left office. But most Americans either feel their finances are worse or about the same as they were when Trump won the 2024 election against Biden’s vice president, Kamala Harris.
Forty-four percent feel their financial situation is worse compared to two years ago, 38 percent feel it’s about the same, and just 18 percent feel it's better.
The annual inflation rate was up 3.7 percent in September — still off the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target rate. The cost of food was up 2.5 percent in September from the year before, according to the federal government’s Consumer Price Index. And energy costs were up a whopping 20.4 percent from last year as Trump’s eight-month-long war in Iran drives up the cost of fuel.
Most voters, including about a quarter of Republicans, think the U.S. made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.
More voters have a slightly better view of the Democratic Party than the Republican Party, as recent polling shows Democrats with a real shot at winning reliably red states.
Forty-six percent of voters have a favorable opinion of the Democratic Party, while 54 percent have an unfavorable opinion. Meanwhile, 41 percent of voters have a favorable opinion of the Republican Party and 59 percent have an unfavorable opinion. Still, neither party has won over a majority of voters.
When asked about their vote for the House of Representatives, 59 percent said Trump was a factor in their decision. Of those voting Democrat, 78 percent said their vote was to oppose Trump. Of those voting Republican, 36 percent said their vote was to support the president, and 62 percent said he was not a factor.
The Democrats will need three House seats and four Senate seats to gain the majority.

sources.text:
Polls start to close in US Mid-Terms, exit polls show Trump at lowest approval rating; Fox projects first senate gain for Dems in Virginia
Washington DC [US], November 4 (ANI): As polling begins to draw to a close in the US Midterms a CBS News Exit poll show that the US President Donald Trump is polling the lowest approval rating for a president in a midterm election. This is currently at 38%.
CBS says that its exit polls show roughly three-quarters of voters are at least dissatisfied with the direction of the country. More voters have negative views of the economy now than they did two years ago,.
The CBS poll says that most Americans think that the U.S. made the wrong decision to take military action in Iran.
President Trump is already bracing for a brutal night. In a Telephonic interview to CBS News before polls closed the US President said, "I have the ultimate power — it's called veto," when he was asked about the prospect of a Democratic-controlled Congress next year.
Trump further said that his veto power could eventually force Democrats to cut bipartisan deals with him, should they make gains.
"Historically, you veto for a couple of months and then they come and say, 'We've got to make a deal,'" Trump told CBS News.
In a post on Truth social, Trump said he was closely following the polls on Fox News.
"Watching the Pre-Election Results on FoxNews, but I can't stand Jessica Tarlov's voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it's the voice that gets me. Have to go somewhere else until that LOSER is off the air — I'll be back later! President DONALD J. TRUMP," he said.
Meanwhile Polls have closed in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia, as well as parts of Indiana and Kentucky, marking some of the first closures of Election Day as voters decide control of Congress and several key gubernatorial and state legislative races.
In a first projection, Fox News reported that Virginia Democrat Senator Mark Warner is projected to win another term in the Senate beating Bert Mizusawa, a former major general in the military who has forayed into politics. (ANI)

Exit Poll Finds 43% Voted to Oppose Trump
sources.text:
Exit Poll Finds 43% Voted to Oppose Trump
Voters didn't just cast ballots on candidates this Election Day; many treated it as a referendum on President Trump. An NBC News national exit poll finds 43% said a key reason for their vote was to oppose Trump, a bigger share than in his first-term midterms in 2018. Only 38% approved of his job performance, with majorities in Senate battlegrounds like Georgia, Ohio, Michigan, and Texas giving him a thumbs-down.
The economy drove much of the backlash. Three-quarters of voters said conditions are poor, and 65% said Trump's policies have made things worse; 62% blamed him for high prices. Inflation and the cost of living dominated concerns. Both parties are viewed more negatively than positively, though Democrats hold an edge on most major issues—and appear to be regaining ground with Latino and under-30 voters. The exit poll suggests Trump's dozens of rallies leading up to the midterms did little to lift his ratings, NBC notes.
The AP Voter Poll had similar findings, with three-quarters of voters saying they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the direction the country is headed in, and roughly the same proportion rating the economy as "not so good" or "poor." Democrats are "cautiously optimistic" about retaking the House and possibly the Senate, the AP reports, though Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on poll results. "I think the results are going to be better than you think," the president predicted in a Fox News interview Tuesday. In the same interview, Trump declared that inflation "is solved."

sources.news_title: Exit polls reveal growing dissatisfaction with Trump, economy
Donald Trump disapproval rating hits 62% as US Midterm initial exit polls show voter dissatisfaction
sources.text:
What do the initial exit polls show about Donald Trump?
The initial exit polls show that the midterms have turned into a referendum on Donald Trump.
- 62% of voters disapprove of Trump while 38% approve.
- 59% of people felt that Trump was a factor in their vote.
- 43% voted against Trump.
- 16% voted in favour of Trump.
The 38% approval rating is the lowest of any sitting president on election day in almost two decades. It was also lower than previous political battles. In the 2018 midterms, 45% of voters approved of his performance and in the 2020 election, 50% approved. The only time his approval rating was lower was in 2008 when George W Bush received 27% approval near the end of his second term.
Immigration policies
Trump’s policies on immigration enforcement have also played a role in deciding how people voted. Initial results from the NBC News Exit Poll show that 57% of people felt Trump had gone too far with his immigration policies. 23% felt it was just right and 21% felt he hadn’t gone far enough. The Trump administration has enforced a crackdown on immigration.
People also had opinions on the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency.
- 59% disapproved.
- 41% approved.
Over 4 in 10 people still approved of Trump’s tough approach or wanted more to be done. Most people had a positive view of immigrants. Overall 59% felt that immigrants do more good than harm to the country.

sources.news_title: Most voters blame Trump for high prices, want Congress to check prez: exit poll
sources.text:
Most voters blame Trump for high prices, want Congress to check prez: exit poll
See more of our coverage in your search results.
WASHINGTON — Exit poll results released Tuesday evening were ominous for Republicans — with 71% of voters saying Congress must do more to check President Trump and 62% blaming him for higher prices.
The early findings by the Associated Press’s Voter Poll showed that 75% of voters were “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the direction of the country and more than six in ten disapproved of Trump’s performance.
Follow for live updates on the 2026 Midterm Elections
Trump has urged midterm voters to act as if he’s on the ballot — a notion that the survey suggests could backfire.
The top issue for voters was the economy, at 39%, followed by the fate of democracy, at 32%, according to the Voter Poll, on which major TV networks collaborated with the AP.
At stake is whether Republicans retain control of the House and Senate for the final two years of Trump’s presidency or whether voters return Democrats to power.
The economy historically has been one of Trump’s strongest areas in polling, but he has struggled to counter the impact of higher energy prices and interest rates, as well as inflation caused by his war with Iran.
The survey found that 46% of voters had a favorable view of the Democratic Party, compared to 41% who said the same of Republicans.
More coverage of the 2026 midterm elections:
Trump had a 38% approval rating, with 62% disapproving.
A devastating 61% of voters said that Trump’s priorities were his personal interests, versus 39% who said he put the country’s interests first.

Relatively few voters (16%) said they voted to show support for Trump while 43% said they did so to oppose him and 41% said it wasn’t a factor when voting for congressional and state officials.
The polling suggests Republicans risk losing both the House and Senate, which would derail Trump’s legislative priorities and nominations while miring his final two years in office in congressional investigations.
Trump, however, is likely to continue flexing his authority to issue executive orders and proclaimed to The Post in a Friday interview that he would become “Mr. Veto” for Democratic bills.
“I guess I’ll become Mr. Veto. I’m not going to let them ruin it,” Trump said when asked about a possible Democratic wave in the election.
“And then at some point, we’ll probably make deals. That’s what’s happened. I mean, this wouldn’t be the first time.”
Trump sought to sway voters with promises of $5,000 checks if Republicans held control of Congress and argued the economy was thriving, pointing to stock-market records and strong employment, greater foreign investment and new manufacturing plants — though his tariffs were a significant headwind for Republicans in some states, particularly along the Canadian border.
He also campaigned on nearly ending illegal border crossings and presiding over a historic drop in violent crime.
But the Iran war and related economic pain, including high gas and diesel prices, weighed on the Republican campaign efforts. Renewed momentum toward a peace deal over the weekend and a significant drop in oil prices Monday came at the final moments of the campaign.

sources.news_title: Nearly half of voters saw midterm election as a rebuke of Trump, NBC News Exit Poll shows
sources.text:
Nearly half of voters say they view the midterm election as an opportunity for a major rebuke of President Donald Trump’s performance, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll.
Forty-three percent said one reason for their votes was to express opposition to Trump — far higher than the share who said the same in the 2018 midterm election during his first term.
The early results show that Trump’s midterm campaign blitz in support of Republican candidates in recent weeks has done little to lift his job approval rating.
A key frustration voters cited? The economy.
Most voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families, with the affordability of gas, food and utilities being a significant concern. Voters blamed Trump for high prices and said his policies are making the economy worse.
The poll was conducted as voters left polling locations across the U.S. on Election Day. Results also include extensive interviews by phone and mail and online with people who voted early or by mail.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections
Trump’s sagging job approval rating
Trump’s job approval rating among voters is lower than the rating of any sitting president on Election Day in nearly two decades, according to the poll.
Thirty-eight percent of voters said they approve of Trump’s performance. That’s substantially lower than in his first midterm election in 2018 (when 45% of voters approved of his performance).
Trump’s dismal approval ratings have dropped in Senate battleground states, as well.
Majorities of Senate voters in Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Texas all said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of his job — also up compared with 2018.
Voters have negative opinions of both parties
Voters expressed more unfavorable than favorable views of the Republican and Democratic parties, the poll showed. And almost 1 in 5 voters said they don’t have favorable opinions of either party — at least 5 percentage points more than the share who said so during the past two midterm elections.
Fifty-four percent of voters Tuesday said they have unfavorable views of the Democratic Party, while 46% have favorable views. For the Republican Party, 59% of voters today said they have unfavorable views, and 41% said they have favorable views. Voters expressed more unfavorable views toward both parties than they did in the last two midterms.
Voters were likelier to say the Democratic Party could better handle several big issues than the Republican Party, including the economy, foreign policy, healthcare and policies about transgender people. The GOP held an advantage on immigration.
On policies related to AI and taxes, voters were split.
Voters also expressed negative opinions about Congress. Three-quarters said they disapproved of the way Congress is handling its job. Republicans were far more likely than Democrats to approve of Congress, 46% to 9%.
Economic pessimism
The economy — once Trump’s strongest issue — is no longer viewed positively by voters, the poll showed.
An overwhelming majority said the nation’s economy is in rough shape (75%) — and 65% said Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. About half of voters casting ballots said the cost of living was crucial to their votes. That is the opposite of how voters viewed the economy in 2018 — a wave election for Democrats during Trump’s first term. That year, 68% of voters said the economy was in good shape.
Voters are driven by the economy
Voters rated the economy as the most important issue facing the country today (39%), followed by the state of democracy (32%), according to the poll. They voiced significant concerns about the prices of gas, groceries and utilities, blaming Trump for affordability problems.
Forty-four percent of voters said their finances are worse today than they were two years ago when Trump returned to office. Just 18% say they’re better off. These numbers are in line with the way voters characterized their finances during the 2022 midterms but much worse than in Trump’s first midterm election in 2018.
Driving voters’ financial concerns: the cost of living. Top issues include the cost of gas and diesel fuel (87% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned), food and groceries (88% concerned), utilities (86%) and healthcare (85%). All told, just under 8 in 10 voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families.
More than half (65%) say Trump’s policies have made the economy worse; 62% said he’s responsible for high prices.
Other key issues for voters: immigration, corruption, Iran and artificial intelligence
More than half of voters (57%) said Trump’s immigration enforcement actions have gone too far, according to the poll. Twenty-three percent said the crackdowns have been about right, and 21% said they have not gone far enough. Fifty-nine percent of voters said they disapproved of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency carrying out much of the enforcement actions; while 41% said they approved.

Corruption was also a key issue. Ninety percent of voters said it was a crucial or major factor in their vote, but they were divided on which party was better positioned to fight it. Thirty-six percent said the Democratic Party, while 31% said Republicans. The remaining third of voters said they didn’t believe either party would be better.
The war in Iran was largely unpopular among voters, with 62% saying the U.S. made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran. Forty-five percent of voters who backed Democratic candidates for the House said the war was crucial to their vote, compared with 21% of voters who supported Republican candidates.
Concerns about AI were also high on voters’ minds: 57% said AI will do more to hurt society than help, the poll showed. A large majority, 76%, said they opposed the construction of a new data center in their community. Voters split almost evenly on which party was better able to handle AI.
Groups we’re watching closely as the night unfolds
We’ll closely watch several groups that helped propel Trump to victory in 2024 — but with particular interest in Latino voters and voters under 30.

After having fallen in every national election since 2018, the share of Latino voters who identify as Democrats ticked up this year to 43% from 39% in 2024, the poll showed.
The share of Latino voters calling themselves independents dropped slightly, to 30% from 32%. The share identifying as Republicans also dropped slightly, to 27% from 29% in 2024.
The results halted a steady erosion of the Democrats’ advantage among Latino voters in party identification, which narrowed from 33 points in 2018 to 10 points in 2024. This year, Democrats hold a 16-point edge.
Young voters also seem to be shifting back to the Democratic Party after Trump shrank the margin among them in the 2024 presidential election.

sources.news_title: Trump Approval at 38% Among Midterm Voters, Preliminary Exit Poll Shows
sources.text:
Trump Approval at 38% Among Midterm Voters, Preliminary Exit Poll Shows
Nearly half of midterm voters said opposing President Donald Trump was one reason they cast ballots Tuesday, according to preliminary results from the NBC News Exit Poll.
In early results released by NBC News, 43% of voters said one reason for their vote was to express opposition to Trump, while 16% said they voted to show support for him.
About 6 in 10 voters said Trump was a factor in their congressional vote. That is slightly lower than in 2018 but well above 2022, when half said President Joe Biden’s performance factored in.
The numbers are preliminary. Exit poll results are updated and reweighted as more interviews arrive through the night, and they are not vote counts or projections of any race.
The survey, conducted by SSRS for a group of news organizations, combines interviews with voters leaving polling places and phone, mail and online interviews with people who voted early or by mail.
Trump’s approval among voters stood at 38%, with 62% disapproving. In his first midterm in 2018, 45% of voters approved of his performance, according to NBC.
NBC’s live coverage noted that 38% is the lowest Election Day approval for a sitting president since 2008, when George W. Bush’s approval among voters fell to 27%.
Majorities of Senate voters in Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Texas said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of his job, the early results showed.
Neither party drew good marks. Fifty-nine percent of voters viewed the Republican Party unfavorably, up from 52% in 2022, while 54% viewed the Democratic Party unfavorably.
Voters were likelier to say Democrats could better handle the economy, foreign policy, health care and government corruption. Republicans held the advantage on immigration, and voters split on taxes and artificial intelligence.
Economy Tops the List
The economy ranked as the most important issue at 39%, followed by the state of democracy at 32%. Three-quarters of voters said the national economy is in rough shape.
Sixty-five percent said Trump’s policies have made the economy worse, and 62% said he is responsible for high prices. Forty-four percent said their finances are worse than two years ago; 18% said better.
The separate AP Voter Poll found a similar picture. About 4 in 10 voters named the economy as the top issue and about 3 in 10 named democracy, while about three-quarters said they were angry or dissatisfied.
On immigration, 57% of voters in the NBC poll said Trump’s enforcement actions have gone too far. Another 23% said they were about right and 21% said they have not gone far enough.
That means more than 4 in 10 voters still back the administration’s approach or want it tougher, even as 59% said they disapprove of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
There was some good news for free-market conservatives. Fifty-seven percent of voters viewed capitalism favorably, compared with 32% for socialism, though voters under 30 favored socialism 47% to 37%.
The share of Latino voters identifying as Democrats rose to 43% from 39% in 2024, while the Republican share slipped to 27% from 29%, according to the poll.
Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters told NBC News Now that Republicans are “well positioned to defy history,” adding that keeping the House “all comes down to turnout.”
Republicans entered Election Day with majorities in both chambers, and the Associated Press reported that the first polls closed at 6 p.m. Eastern in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. No House or Senate race had been called when the exit poll results were released.

The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Donald Trump said on Tuesday. 
The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years. 
Trump said Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the US to spend. But Trump also said that US aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel. 
Even far-right conservatives, who have supported Trump in the past, have taken issue with US support for Israel, with prominent commentators like Tucker Carlson openly questioning the value of the relationship. 
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.” 
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu’s office. But at least some of his political opponents were cautious. 
Opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said the announcement showed that Netanyahu must go. 
"The fact that Israel's defense establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct is. He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced," Eisenkot said in a statement. 
Yair Golan, a leader in Israel’s opposition bloc, said an end to US military aid would deal a “severe blow to Israel’s security” at a time when the country is fighting wars on multiple fronts.  
“The burden of funding defense needs at such a critical juncture will fall entirely upon the Israeli public,” Golan, a former deputy military chief, said in a statement. 
The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years. 
In 2016, President Barack Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel’s ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries. 
Netanyahu has talked about the need to wean Israel off the aid in the past and has said that the American aid would end at some point. 
He told The Economist in January that he wanted to “taper off” US military aid in the next 10 years and that such a change was “in the works.” 
But the optics of the aid had also become an issue, according to Trump, who singled out El-Sayed for using it as a talking point. 
“The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” Trump said Tuesday on Fox. “And we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we’ve agreed. He was very understanding of it.” 
Phasing out direct military and economic aid to Israel has long been a subject of debate in both countries and has gained traction in the last several years. 
There are several issues that complicate it, though, not least of which are obligations the US has to Israel under the terms of the Camp David peace accords with Egypt, which require the United States to support Israel and Egypt with security assistance. 
In addition, much of the assistance the US provides Israel comes in the form of foreign military financing, or FMF, that gives Israel the money but requires it to spend the money on American-produced weaponry, meaning the funds are plowed back into the US economy. 
Unless Israel plans to spend the same amount on purchasing American materiel, US defense contractors may see an impact. 
An academic study published last year showed the US under the administrations of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza war in 2023. The study was published on the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict. 
Another study, also published last year by the Costs of War project at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs, said the US had spent roughly $10 billion more on security aid and operations in the broader Middle East in the previous two years. 
While the reports relied on open source material for most of their findings, they offered some of the most comprehensive accountings of US military aid to close ally Israel and estimated costs of direct American military involvement in the Middle East.

sources.news_title: Midterm Voters Turn Election Into a Referendum on Trump, NBC Exit Poll Finds
sources.text:
International-News
Midterm Voters Turn Election Into a Referendum on Trump, NBC Exit Poll Finds
Economic anxiety and frustration over persistent inflation helped shape the electorate, with a striking share of voters casting their ballots primarily to oppose President Donald Trump and his policies
For millions of Americans, the midterm elections were about far more than congressional races. They became a direct verdict on President Donald Trump.
According to the NBC News Exit Poll, 43% of voters said their primary motivation was to oppose Trump, a figure that underscores the degree to which the president dominated the political landscape even in an election traditionally centered on local races and congressional control. The number is notably higher than the level recorded during the 2018 midterm elections held during Trump’s first term, highlighting the extent to which voter sentiment has become focused on the White House.
The findings suggest that many voters approached Election Day less as a choice between competing candidates than as an opportunity to register approval or disapproval of the president’s leadership and agenda.
Driving much of that frustration was the economy, particularly the continued pressure of high prices on household budgets. Inflation emerged as one of the dominant concerns cited by voters, with rising costs for fuel, groceries and utility bills remaining a persistent source of financial strain.
The poll indicates that many voters directly linked those economic pressures to the administration. Respondents broadly attributed elevated prices to Trump’s policies, reflecting a belief that White House decisions have played a significant role in shaping current economic conditions.
The combination of economic unease and political dissatisfaction appears to have transformed the midterm elections into a broader judgment on the president’s stewardship of the country, offering a snapshot of an electorate that remains deeply focused on the cost of living and increasingly willing to hold political leaders accountable for it.
